13 What is the torque of the couple shown?
15 N
15.0 cm
5.0 cm
15 N
A
0.75 N m
B
1.50 N m
C
3.00 N m
D
5.25 N m

hints: Notice the two $15 \text{ N}$ forces are opposite in direction and separated by only $5.0 \text{ cm}$, not the $15.0 \text{ cm}$ marked from the left end.
Recall torque of a couple is one force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the forces: $\text{torque} = Fd$.
Convert the $5.0 \text{ cm}$ separation to metres before multiplying by $15 \text{ N}$ to get $\text{N m}$.
walkthrough: Identify the couple: a $15 \text{ N}$ force up and a $15 \text{ N}$ force down, so resultant force is zero but turning effect is non-zero.
Find the perpendicular distance between the lines of action from the diagram: the upward force and downward force are $5.0 \text{ cm}$ apart.
State the rule for a couple: $\text{torque} = F \times d$, where $F$ is one of the forces and $d$ is their separation.
Convert distance to SI units: $d = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.050 \text{ m}$.
The $15.0 \text{ cm}$ mark locates the upper force from the left end and is not part of the couple separation. This is option A

A.explanation: Torque is $15 \text{ N} \times 0.050 \text{ m} = 0.75 \text{ N m}$ using the $5.0 \text{ cm}$ separation between the two forces.

B.explanation: This doubles the correct value, as if the $5.0 \text{ cm}$ separation were $10.0 \text{ cm}$.

C.explanation: This uses the full $20.0 \text{ cm}$ length instead of the $5.0 \text{ cm}$ perpendicular distance between the two $15 \text{ N}$ forces.

D.explanation: This incorrectly combines the $15.0 \text{ cm}$ and $5.0 \text{ cm}$ distances instead of using only the separation of the couple.
